WHERE ACCELERATION STARTS

Urban tasks do not grow exponentially on their own. Acceleration comes from an industry that reinvests, expands capacity and can deliver more robots. Every sector retains human tasks.

WHAT WE REPRESENT

Each unit is an equivalent task in the scenario. A person performs many tasks: covering one does not eliminate their profession. People can move to other tasks, which this scene does not calculate.

Illustrative hypotheses · no dates, Tesla figures or employment forecasts.

One city, three hypotheses.

We start with 600 equivalent human tasks across six sectors. Industry starts separately with 24 robots and six facilities. Every robot sent to the city becomes unavailable for work in that industry. Transit takes one illustrative cycle.

Urban allocation is automatic and balances relative sector coverage. Each hypothesis sets different sector limits: model parameters, not published estimates. Not all care, health or education tasks are automated.

The city counts covered tasks, not economic productivity or eliminated jobs. It does not calculate demand, wages, prices, service quality, regulation or new occupations. Robot capabilities assume the selected tasks are technically feasible. Charging and shifts are omitted at this aggregate scale. Industrial resources, construction and limits are preserved in the regional model.
